title: SPACE – Study on the Psychological and Affective Consequences and neurobiological Effects of Environmental, social, and interpersonal influences on mental well-being and brain function
summary:
Some people grow up under difficult circumstances, for example, in a stressful family environment or in a densely populated city. Such experiences can have long-term effects on how they experience stress, feelings like anger or anxiety, and everyday behavior.
The peripersonal space—the area directly around our bodies—is particularly important in this regard. When other people get very close to us, it can be perceived as unpleasant or threatening. For some people, this can lead more quickly to stress, strong emotions, or even aggressive behavior.
It is not yet fully understood which psychological, physical, and brain-related processes contribute to the fact that early adverse experiences are later associated with increased irritability or aggressive behavior.
This study investigates how early adverse experiences influence the experience of stress, strong negative emotions, and aggressive behavior in everyday life. The long-term goal is to better understand why some people react more strongly to stress or closeness than others, in order to develop new approaches to prevention and support.
The study involves adolescents and young adults, with and without adverse childhood experiences or growing up in a large city.
In addition to virtual reality, imaging techniques, genetic analyses, neuropsychological testing, and questionnaires, we also use innovative m-health technology. This mobile technology allows us to identify, under real-life conditions, the factors that influence the relationship between everyday experiences, physical reactions, and brain activity—all the way through to psychiatric disorders.
conditions: Problems related to negative life events in childhood

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
- participants aged 16 years and older: Ability to understand the study protocol and provide fully informed consent, as well as the ability to use self-rating scales.
- participants aged 14-15 years: additional informed consent by the legal guardians
- assignment of study participants to the URB+/URB- groups: Exposure to early-life urbanicity based on the participants’ place(s) of residence from birth to 14 years of age. To do so, we use population categories from the epidemiologic literature, weighed by the number of years spent in each category. The final proxy scores for URB are between 14 and 42, whereby participants with values between 14-21 are assigned to the URB- group and those with values between 22-42 to the URB+ group.
- assignment of study participants to the ACE+ /ACE- groups: Presence or absence of ACE based on severity ratings in the Maltreatment Classification System (e.g., ACE+ : MCS severity cut-off scores for physical neglect bigger than or equal 2 and/or physical abuse bigger than or equal 1 and/or emotional neglect/abuse bigger than or equal 2) 
- Willingness to use the provided devices of ambulant assessment (e.g. smartphone, sensors)
- Sufficient understanding of the German language
Exclusion criteria:
1) Lifetime history of DSM-5 bipolar disorder, schizophrenia or schizophrenia spectrum disorder or substance dependence other than nicotine dependence. Severe alcohol and cannabis use disorder will be excluded.
2) History of severe head trauma or other severe central nervous system disorder (e.g., Parkinson’s disease, multiple sclerosis)
3) For the ACE-/URB+ and ACE-/URB- groups: Exposure to any form of significant ACE.
4) Pregnancy or nursing infants
5) Standard MRI exclusion criteria as set forth by the internal user policy
6) Current use of medications or drugs known to interact with the CNS within at least four half-lives post last intake
